# ForgeMark

**A concurrent git push/clone throughput benchmark for any smart-HTTP git forge.**

ForgeMark measures **sustained push or clone throughput and per-operation
latency** the way an agent fleet hits a forge: many concurrent writers, readers,
or mixed sessions. It drives **real git operations** through
[`go-git`](https://github.com/go-git/go-git) (packfile build + ref update for
pushes, upload-pack for clones), so it exercises the forge paths directly — not
a synthetic HTTP approximation.

It works against **any smart-HTTP git host** — GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket,
self-hosted, GitHub Enterprise Server, github.com, and
[Entire](https://github.com/entireio). There's no target flag: the forge is
inferred from `-remote` (and, for Entire, from the auth flags you supply).

> **Only run ForgeMark against infrastructure you own or are explicitly
> authorized to load-test.** A tight push loop is abusive traffic to a host that
> hasn't agreed to it.

## Install

```bash
go install github.com/entireio/forgemark/cmd/forgemark@latest
```

## Web GUI

`forgemark serve` starts a local dashboard over the same engine: configure a
run in the browser, watch live per-second throughput / latency-percentile /
error charts while it executes, and benchmark **multiple forges side by side**
— every concurrency level starts simultaneously on all targets, so the overlay
is a fair comparison.

```bash
forgemark serve            # http://127.0.0.1:8377
```

- **Try it with no forge**: add a `demo://` target (e.g.
  `demo://fast?p50=60ms&spread=3&err=0.01&cap=400`) — a synthetic latency
  generator that exercises the whole pipeline offline. Add two with different
  profiles to see the comparison view.
- **Targets** take the same parameters as the CLI flags (remote, repos, object
  format, and the Entire fields). The credential is never typed into the
  browser: each target names a **source** — `gh CLI login` / `glab CLI login` /
  `entire CLI login` — and the server reads the token from that
  already-authenticated CLI at run start, so it never enters the page or the
  request body. (For GitLab the server uses glab's git-credential helper, which
  returns a repository-scoped token even when glab's stored API token isn't.)
  **Add from CLI logins** prefills complete GitHub / GitLab / Entire targets
  (endpoints, repos, credential source) from whichever CLIs you're logged into,
  and the **⚡ Push race preset** fills the race workload and opens the race
  view. A forge without a supported CLI login is benchmarked from the command
  line (`forgemark -token-file …`), not the web form.
- **History** lists every result doc in `results/` — CLI runs included — and
  overlays any selection as ops/s-vs-concurrency and p95-vs-concurrency curves.
  Server runs also store their 1-second live series, so finished runs replay.
- The server binds to loopback by default and refuses cross-origin requests.
  It is a load-generation control panel: the same authorization warning as the
  CLI applies, and starting a run requires confirming it in the form.

`-addr` changes the listen address (a warning prints if it isn't loopback);
`-results` points at a different results directory.

Yes, pushing under a namespace outside `refs/heads/` is the cleanest client-side lever, and the code is close to supporting it. A few things worth weighing before picking it.

**Why a non-branch ref works.** Forge indexers, code search, CI triggers and branch UIs almost all key off `refs/heads/*` and `refs/tags/*`. A ref like `refs/forgemark/fm…-c1-a0` still goes through the full receive-pack path on the server, so the benchmark still measures packfile unpack, ref CAS and hooks. It just never becomes a branch, so nothing downstream picks it up. It also sidesteps the "first push promotes a branch to HEAD and then the forge refuses to delete it" problem that the sweep currently has to special-case.

**The trade-offs:**

- **It changes what you measure.** If Entire does indexing or any post-receive work synchronously in the push path, non-branch refs skip that cost and the numbers get rosier than what a real agent pushing a branch would see. If it is async, push latency is unaffected but you stop generating the downstream load, which may or may not be something you want to benchmark.
- **Forge acceptance varies.** GitHub, GitLab and Gitea all accept arbitrary `refs/*` namespaces, but each reserves some (`refs/pull/*` on GitHub and Gitea, `refs/merge-requests/*`, `refs/keep-around/*`, `refs/pipelines/*` on GitLab). A dedicated name like `refs/forgemark/` avoids all of those. Whether Entire accepts it is something to confirm against your receive-pack.
- **Session strategy clones need a branch.** The clone and session paths clone `-base-ref`, which defaults to the remote default branch. Push-only runs are fine, but if a repo never gets a branch, the clone strategy needs an explicit base ref or a seeded repo.

**Forge-side alternatives** that keep the workload representative and only need Entire changes:

- **Exclude by author.** Every bench commit already uses the fixed `authorEmail` constant and `agent-N` author names, so the indexer could skip those commits outright.
- **Exclude by branch prefix.** Runs already take `-branch-prefix`, so Entire could treat `bench/` or similar as unindexed.
- **Exclude by repo.** A bench org or a per-repo "no search index" flag is the bluntest and most reliable option.

**If you want the ref-namespace route in forgemark**, the `refs/heads/` assumption lives in a handful of places: `DestRef` in `internal/bench/config.go`, the stale-ref regex and default-branch sparing in `internal/bench/cleanup.go`, the push refspecs in `agent.go` and `session.go`, and the error-normalizing `reRef` regex in `agent.go`. A `-ref-namespace` flag defaulting to `refs/heads/` would keep current behaviour and let you opt into a hidden namespace per run.

**My recommendation:** do both. Add the namespace flag so GitHub and GitLab comparisons stay clean without asking anything of those forges, and add the author-email exclusion on the Entire side so you can still run branch-shaped pushes against Entire when you want the full post-receive cost included.

No. In the session strategy the only thing that stays a branch is the one you clone from, and that is the repo's real default branch which forgemark never writes to.

Two refs are in play per session:

- **Read side:** `cloneSession` clones the remote default branch, or `-base-ref`. That is pre-existing content like `main`. It would stay `refs/heads/...` and nothing forgemark does touches it.
- **Write side:** `runSessions` builds the destination as `a.ref` plus `-sN` and pushes with the refspec `+<local branch>:<that ref>`. Today `a.ref` comes from `DestRef`, which hardcodes `refs/heads/`. If `DestRef` emitted `refs/forgemark/...` instead, the session checkpoints would land at `refs/forgemark/fm…-c1-a0-s3`. The forge only sees the destination side of the refspec, so the fact that the local source is `refs/heads/master` or the cloned head is irrelevant to it.

So the session strategy needs no extra work beyond the namespace change in `DestRef` and the matching regexes in cleanup. The clone side keeps hitting a real branch, and the pushed checkpoints are hidden refs.

The caveat I raised earlier only applies to an unseeded repo. Today the first bench push to an empty repo creates a default branch, which later sessions clone. With a hidden namespace the repo stays unborn, so `cloneSession` takes its existing `ErrEmptyRemoteRepository` path and commits on an orphan with no read load. Against a repo seeded with a normal `main` that path never triggers.
yeah but in session it never pushes to the default right?

Right. Session pushes go to `<run>-c<level>-a<agent>-s<N>` and then delete that ref at the end of each session. The default branch is never a push target.

With one exception: against an empty repo, the very first session push creates the only branch, so the forge promotes it to HEAD. The cleanup comment in `cleanup.go` describes this. That ref then survives, because the forge refuses to delete its current branch, and it stays the default forever. On a seeded repo this never happens.

So whether that matters for your search pollution depends on what Entire ingests:

- **Only the default branch:** session on a seeded repo is already clean today, and the branch strategy is the only polluter. No ref-namespace change needed, just never run against an unseeded repo.
- **Every branch on push:** session pollutes too, since each `-sN` ref is a real branch for the seconds it exists. Deleting it afterwards only helps if the indexer also removes content on ref delete. If it doesn't, the hidden namespace or the author-email exclusion is still needed.

Worth checking which of those Entire does before changing forgemark.
that one head branch is fine for session strategy. we are doing this to avoid rate limits and spending money on search ingestions

That changes the calculus: the point is to not trigger the ingest at all, not to keep the index tidy. Then the ref namespace is the right lever, and the author-email idea is the wrong one, since it still fires the pipeline before anything gets filtered.

One thing to verify on the Entire side before building it: that the ingest trigger keys off `refs/heads/*` and not every ref update receive-pack reports. If it fires on any ref, a hidden namespace buys nothing and you need a repo-level or namespace-level exclusion in the trigger itself. Also confirm receive-pack accepts a custom namespace at all.

If that checks out, the forgemark change is small:

- **`DestRef` in `config.go`** takes the namespace instead of hardcoding `refs/heads/`. Session refs inherit it automatically since they append `-sN` to that value.
- **`staleBenchRefRe` and `sweepSpecs` in `cleanup.go`** match on the same namespace. The default-branch sparing stays, it just becomes a no-op for hidden refs.
- **`reRef` in `agent.go`** widens so error grouping still collapses the volatile ref.
- **A `-ref-namespace` flag** defaulting to `refs/heads/`, plus the field on the server target form so the Entire preset and compare scripts set `refs/forgemark/`.

Keeping `refs/heads/` as the default means GitHub and GitLab runs keep measuring the branch-shaped push a real agent does, and only the targets where ingestion costs money opt out. The numbers across forges stop being strictly apples to apples when one side skips post-receive work, so the result doc should record the namespace per target.

The one-head-branch behaviour you are fine with goes away under the hidden namespace, since no branch is ever created. On an empty repo session clones would take the orphan path with no read load, so those repos want a seeded `main`.

Fair point. Receive-pack does the same work for `refs/forgemark/x` as for `refs/heads/x`: same pack unpack, same ref CAS, same connectivity check. The only thing that differs is what the forge kicks off afterwards, and on GitHub and GitLab that is async and never shows up in the measured push latency. So "branch-shaped" is not a real distinction for the number forgemark reports, and the default-branch promotion on empty repos was the only visible side effect.

That makes the simpler design the better one:

- **Default to `refs/forgemark/` for every forge.** The comparison stays apples to apples, no bench branches show up in anyone's branch list or search, and Entire skips the ingest.
- **Keep `-ref-namespace` as an override** for someone who explicitly wants branch-shaped pushes, for example to load a forge's post-receive pipeline on purpose.
- **Document that an empty repo stays empty.** No branch is ever created, so session and clone strategies against an unseeded repo degrade to the orphan path with no read load. Seed a `main` first.

Still worth confirming Entire's receive-pack accepts the namespace and that its ingest trigger ignores it. Everything else is the file list from before.

- **Result docs did not record the namespace.** The reviewer was right, and my earlier PR text overstated this. Only the live status payload carried it, not the persisted doc. The CLI banner also prints the namespace at run start.
- **The sweep stranded legacy `refs/heads/` leftovers.** The regex now always alternates `refs/heads/` alongside the configured namespace, with the same shape, prefix and age guards. Default-branch sparing is unchanged, which matters because a legacy run may have promoted a bench ref to HEAD on an empty repo. Other custom namespaces are still never crossed into.

**Verification:** build, vet, race tests and golangci-lint are clean. New tests cover the legacy-namespace alternation including capture-group position, result-doc round trip, and legacy normalization for both doc formats.
